planting.note: Divide and pot in a peat-based, moisture-retentive mix in spring; its smaller mature size fits tabletop pots and smaller hanging baskets on a shaded zone 9-12 porch or lanai year-round.

directions: This dwarf sport of 'Bostoniensis' holds its pinnae shorter, denser, and more tightly bunched, forming a rounded mound less than half the size of the standard Boston fern already in this dataset. Fronds emerge upright and arch only slightly rather than cascading, giving it a neater, more compact silhouette well suited to smaller containers. It shares the species' need for constant moisture and high humidity, dropping pinnules quickly if allowed to dry or sit in dry indoor air.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension Foliage Plant Production Guide
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder

planting.note: Plant divisions in humus-rich, evenly moist potting mix in spring shade; this heirloom cultivar tolerates lower humidity than many Boston fern selections, making it dependable for covered porches in zone 9-12.

directions: Introduced in the early twentieth century and named for Theodore Roosevelt, this heirloom cultivar bears broader, more open pinnae than standard 'Bostoniensis', with wavy, crested, and occasionally forked tips that give each frond a feathery, ruffled texture distinct from the tightly cut 'Fluffy Ruffles' already in this dataset. It also tolerates somewhat lower ambient humidity than many Boston fern selections, making it a more forgiving choice for outdoor covered porches.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
American Fern Society

common_name: Lemon Button Fern (Duffii Fern, Ball Fern)

planting.note: Divide small clumps into shallow pots or terrarium beds in spring; its dwarf scale makes it a popular dish-garden and terrarium fern as well as a shaded groundcover in zone 9-11.

directions: A dwarf sport of the tuberous sword fern, this cultivar produces tightly packed, nearly round button-shaped pinnae along short wiry fronds, forming a dense low mound entirely unlike the elongated straplike fronds of the species or the finely cut foliage of 'Rooseveltii'. Crushed foliage carries a faint lemon scent, and small fuzzy tubers form along the soil surface. Its diminutive scale makes it a favorite terrarium and dish-garden fern rather than a landscape specimen.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension
Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Mount on a wood slab, tree-fern fiber panel, or wire basket lined with sphagnum moss rather than potting in soil; mist regularly and fertilize monthly in the growing season to replicate humid Philippine rainforest conditions.

directions: Long confused with Platycerium superbum, this Philippine and Southeast Asian species produces a single non-suckering crown of deeply lobed, antler-like fertile fronds that can arch outward more than five feet from broad, overlapping shield fronds clasping the mount. Unlike the clumping bifurcatum already in this dataset, grande never produces offset pups, so each plant remains a solitary specimen that slowly builds an ever-larger basal shield mass over many years.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
American Fern Society

planting.note: Mount on a cork or tree-fern slab lined with sphagnum in a warm, humid microclimate such as a greenhouse or enclosed shade structure, out of direct wind; it resents drying out or cold drafts more than other staghorns.

directions: Native to the humid forests of Madagascar, this species is instantly recognizable by the raised, netted, diamond-patterned venation pressed across its rounded shield fronds, a texture unlike the smooth or lobed shields of any other Platycerium in this dataset. Its narrow, once-forked fertile fronds are proportionally small compared to the dominant shield, and the whole plant stays compact and slow-growing, prized by specialist growers for its sculptural shield texture.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
American Fern Society

planting.note: Mount on a wood slab or hang in a sphagnum-lined basket in bright filtered light; more sun- and drought-tolerant than P. bifurcatum, so it can handle a brighter porch or lanai exposure.

directions: Native to Queensland and New Guinea, Platycerium hillii closely resembles the common P. bifurcatum already in this dataset but holds its fertile fronds more upright and stiffly, with narrower, less deeply divided antler tips and thicker, glossier shield fronds that resist drying out in brighter exposures. It tends to stay more compact than bifurcatum and forms tighter clusters of basal offsets over time.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
American Fern Society

planting.note: Mount on wood or in a wire basket lined with sphagnum; readily produces basal pups that can be left attached to form a spreading colony or divided off for propagation.

directions: Native to Madagascar and East Africa, this species produces rounded, gently lobed shield fronds and shallowly forked, felted gray-green fertile fronds with a soft, woolly texture from dense star-shaped hairs, distinguishing it from the smoother-fronded bifurcatum and veitchii already in this dataset. It clusters and pups freely at the base, gradually building into a multi-crown colony rather than remaining a solitary specimen.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
American Fern Society

planting.note: Mount in a brighter, more open spot than other staghorns and let the mount dry between waterings; its native seasonally dry Andean habitat makes it markedly more drought-tolerant than typical rainforest staghorns.

directions: The only Platycerium native to South America, found in the seasonally dry forests of Peru and Bolivia, this species produces long, narrow, undivided strap-like fertile fronds that hang straight down rather than forking into antler tips like every other staghorn fern in this dataset. Its shield fronds are smaller and more tightly appressed to the mount, reflecting its adaptation to a drier, more sun-exposed native habitat than its rainforest relatives.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
American Fern Society

common_name: Elephant Ear Staghorn Fern (Ellis's Staghorn Fern)

planting.note: Mount on a large slab to accommodate its broad, fan-shaped shields; provide bright filtered light and consistent humidity typical of eastern Madagascar's rainforest margins.

directions: Endemic to a small region of eastern Madagascar, this species produces unusually broad, rounded, overlapping shield fronds that fan outward like a pair of elephant ears, distinct from the narrower or more deeply lobed shields of other Madagascan staghorns in this dataset. Its fertile fronds are wide and gently pendulous rather than sharply forked, giving the whole plant a softer, more rounded silhouette.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
American Fern Society

planting.note: Mount and keep in higher humidity and lower light than other staghorns to mimic the deep rainforest understory of West and Central Africa; avoid direct sun, which scorches the thin shield fronds.

directions: Native to the rainforest understory of West and Central Africa, this species is named for its distinctive triangular, flat-pressed shield fronds that closely hug the mount rather than cupping outward. Its narrow fertile fronds fork only at the very tips into a small number of antler points, a markedly simpler branching pattern than the heavily divided fronds of bifurcatum or veitchii already in this dataset.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
American Fern Society

planting.note: Provide cooler winter temperatures and better air movement than lowland tropical staghorns to mimic its native Himalayan foothill and cloud-forest habitat; propagate only from spore or division since it is endangered in the wild.

directions: Found from the Himalayan foothills through Southeast Asia, this staghorn is notable for its thin, softly drooping fertile fronds with narrow, deeply cut segments that hang in a loose curtain rather than standing upright like most other Platycerium species in this dataset. Its shield fronds develop a papery, tan-brown texture as they age and overlap in layers, a coloration not seen in the greener shields of bifurcatum or hillii.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
American Fern Society
PMC/NCBI: Complete Chloroplast Genome of Platycerium wallichii

planting.note: Start on a very large, sturdy mount from the outset since this is the largest-growing staghorn species; best suited to spacious greenhouse or lanai settings rather than small patios.

directions: Native to New Guinea, this is the largest-growing species in the genus, ultimately producing shield fronds and antler-like fertile fronds far exceeding those of the already-large P. superbum in this dataset. Young plants resemble superbum, but mature specimens develop broader, more heavily overlapping shields and can eventually weigh many dozens of pounds, making it a specimen plant for only the most spacious shaded settings.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
American Fern Society

planting.note: Mount in bright, humid, warm conditions typical of lowland Southeast Asian rainforest; avoid disturbing the hollow shield chambers, which in nature house ant colonies that fertilize the fern, and water through the small openings at the shield tips.

directions: Found in the lowland rainforests of Thailand, Malaysia, and Borneo, this staghorn has evolved one of the most unusual growth forms in the genus: its shield fronds curl inward to form closed, hollow chambers rather than overlapping flat plates, creating nesting cavities for symbiotic ant colonies. Its upright, narrowly forked fertile fronds stand well above the shield in a distinctly vertical, antler-like arrangement unlike the broader, more horizontal fronds of other Platycerium species in this dataset.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
American Fern Society

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich, well-draining soil or mount as an epiphyte in a shaded, humid spot; it is more cold-tolerant than the similar Asplenium nidus, handling brief cool spells in warm-temperate zone 9 gardens.

directions: Native to Australia and Pacific islands, this species is often confused with and sold under the name Asplenium nidus already in this dataset, but grows considerably larger, with undivided, glossy strap-shaped fronds reaching up to five feet and a distinctive raised keel running beneath the midrib. Its rosette is broader and more upright than true nidus, and it tolerates cooler nighttime temperatures better, making it hardier for outdoor zone 9-11 shade gardens.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
Atlas of Living Australia

planting.note: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-draining soil in a sheltered shady spot; it is one of the parent species of the popular hybrid Asplenium 'Austral Gem' and shares that hybrid's tolerance for average home humidity.

directions: Endemic to Norfolk Island, this species is unusual among Asplenium for producing two distinct frond forms on the same plant, as its name suggests: simple, leathery, undivided fronds alongside more deeply cut, pinnatifid fronds with narrow lobed segments. This dimorphic habit sets it clearly apart from the uniformly undivided fronds of the bird's nest ferns already in this dataset and from the uniformly bipinnate fronds of Asplenium bulbiferum.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
Norfolk Island National Park

planting.note: Grow in a well-draining, slightly chunky potting mix with a support, trellis, or hanging basket for its vigorous trailing stems; pinch tips to encourage a fuller cascade.

directions: A vigorous New World tropical vine, this species produces thin, wiry stems lined with small, glossy, heart-shaped leaves that trail or climb considerably farther than the stiffer, more restrained scandens already in this dataset. Its thinner, more delicate leaf texture and faster growth rate make it a popular choice for dense hanging curtains rather than the tidier mounded look of rosette peperomias.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Pot in a well-draining, chunky mix and let the surface dry between waterings; its creeping stems root readily at the nodes, making it easy to propagate by division or stem cuttings.

directions: Native to tropical Central and South America and the West Indies, this low-creeping species bears dull bronze-green, rounded leaves deeply quilted by sunken yellowish veins, a texture giving the foliage a shell-like, beetle-back appearance distinct from the smoother rippled leaves of the caperata cultivars already in this dataset. It forms a low, dense mat useful as an underplanting in shaded containers.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder

planting.note: Grow in bright, filtered light rather than deep shade to maintain its red stem color and compact habit, in a fast-draining mix that dries slightly between waterings.

directions: This upright, bushy species is distinguished by hairy, bright red stems bearing tight whorls of small, olive-green leaves etched with a fine network of silvery veins and flushed crimson on their undersides. Its columnar, densely whorled growth habit is unlike any of the trailing, rosette, or broad-leaved peperomias already present in this dataset, giving it a distinctly textural, almost conifer-like silhouette.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Pot in a fast-draining succulent-friendly mix and let the soil dry between waterings; its thick, fleshy leaves store water and rot readily if kept too wet, so it tolerates brighter, drier positions than most peperomias.

directions: Bearing thick, glossy, spoon-shaped leaves that curl gently at the edges and resemble miniature magnolia foliage, this shrubby, upright species forms a dense clump considerably sturdier and more succulent-textured than the thinner leaves of obtusifolia already in this dataset. Its tolerance for brief drying and brighter light makes it more forgiving of average indoor conditions than most shade-loving peperomias.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) Plant Finder
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Grow in a fast-draining succulent mix with bright indirect light, letting the soil dry fully between waterings; a small trellis or a pot edge for the stems to trail over suits its climbing habit.

directions: A succulent climbing species from the high-elevation forests of Peru, this peperomia produces small, dark green, keel-shaped leaves folded almost in half along their length, a fleshy, angular leaf form unlike the flat, rounded, or heart-shaped leaves of the other peperomias already in this dataset. Its wiry, clustering stems and drought tolerance suit a bright windowsill or succulent-style terrarium better than consistently moist shade conditions.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot or terrarium with a well-draining, humus-rich mix; its creeping, node-rooting stems propagate easily and work well as a low groundcover in shaded terrarium plantings.

directions: This creeping, mat-forming species produces thick, fleshy, broadly rounded leaves held in tight clusters that appear whorled due to very short internodes, though the leaves are technically arranged in opposite pairs. Its dense, low, succulent-leaved mat habit is more compact and tightly packed than the wiry, wide-spaced trailing stems of rotundifolia or prostrata already in this dataset, making it a popular choice for closed terrariums and paludariums.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
USDA GRIN Taxonomy for Plants
